hints.junior: "esbuild is faster" is an assertion, not an explanation — the real reasons are architectural, not a webpack misconfiguration.
hints.mid: Webpack's loader chain runs each module through separately-authored JS functions in a single, JIT-warming Node process — that's the actual bottleneck, not a setting to tune.
hints.staff: esbuild optimizes for raw throughput at the cost of the flexibility webpack's loader/plugin model optimizes for — neither is doing it wrong.

hints.junior: Toggle between the two pipelines and watch how each processes the same simulated 400 modules — the numbers are illustrative of the mechanism, not a real benchmark.
hints.mid: webpack mode processes modules one loader stage at a time in a single thread — esbuild mode fans them out across simulated cores in far fewer passes.
hints.staff: Watch which stage each pipeline spends its time in — webpack bottlenecks on the loader chain; esbuild has no comparably expensive stage to bottleneck on.

hints.junior: esbuild is written in Go and compiled to native code, so it runs at full speed immediately — no JavaScript engine warm-up needed.
hints.mid: esbuild touches each file's AST only about three times total; a webpack loader chain re-parses and re-serializes once per loader in that chain.
hints.staff: Go's shared-memory threads make esbuild's internal parallelism cheap to coordinate — a Node bundler doing real multi-core work pays real serialization overhead between worker threads.

hints.junior: esbuild plugins only get two real hooks, onResolve and onLoad — they can't rewrite arbitrary JS the way a webpack loader or Babel plugin can.
hints.mid: webpack's decade-plus head start shows up as ecosystem maturity — Module Federation, persistent caching, and loaders for nearly every asset type already exist.
hints.staff: Most "esbuild vs webpack" comparisons are really comparing a tool built on esbuild, like Vite, against a from-scratch webpack config — not esbuild's bare CLI against webpack's dev server.

sections.junior: Today's case looks at why esbuild's dev rebuilds are so much faster than webpack's, and why that's an architecture question, not a tuning one.
sections.mid: Webpack's pipeline runs every module through a chain of separately authored loader functions, all inside a single JavaScript process that has to warm up before it runs fast.
sections.staff: esbuild optimizes for raw throughput. Webpack's loader and plugin model optimizes for flexibility. Those are different goals, not one tool doing it wrong.

sections.junior: esbuild is written in Go and compiled to native code, so it runs at full speed right away, with no warm-up period the way a JavaScript program has.
sections.mid: It also touches each file's syntax tree only a handful of times in total, instead of re-parsing it once per loader in a chain.
sections.staff: Go's threads share memory directly, so esbuild can coordinate real parallel work cheaply, in a way a JavaScript bundler using worker threads can't.

sections.junior: Try toggling between the two pipelines and watch how each one works through the same set of simulated modules.
sections.mid: Notice webpack's time is dominated by one particular stage, while esbuild doesn't really have an equivalent bottleneck.
sections.staff: The numbers here are meant to be illustrative of the mechanism. They're not a benchmark of any particular real project.

sections.junior: esbuild is faster because it's a genuinely different kind of program, not because webpack is set up wrong.
sections.mid: The speed comes from native code, far fewer passes over the code, and real parallelism, which is why tools like Vite use esbuild specifically for the dev-time step.
sections.staff: esbuild's plugin surface is real but narrower, so most teams keep webpack or Rollup for production and use esbuild where its speed actually matters, the inner dev loop.
